faq.a: It quickly narrows the differential diagnosis of anaemia, allowing targeted, affordable tests.
faq.q: Why is MCV important in a low‑resource setting?

faq.a: Yes, chronic haemolysis and iron loss from repeated infections often lead to micro‑cytic anaemia.
faq.q: Can malaria cause a low MCV?

faq.a: Use a peripheral smear to assess cell size qualitatively and rely on clinical clues.
faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot measure MCV?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has Hb 8 g/dL and MCV 70 fL — what is the most likely diagnosis and next test? — Iron‑deficiency anaemia; order serum ferritin.
A patient on zidovudine presents with fatigue, MCV 115 fL, and normal Hb — how do you manage the macro‑cytosis? — Review drug necessity; switch if possible; check B12/folate to exclude deficiency.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a child has anaemia, MCV 78 fL, and a positive stool occult blood test — what does this indicate? — Iron loss from chronic GI bleeding; treat iron deficiency and investigate source.
A 55‑year‑old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy has MCV 105 fL, peripheral neuropathy, and low B12 — what is the priority? — Replace B12 urgently to prevent irreversible neuropathy.
How does a high RDW help when MCV is normal? — It suggests mixed aetiology (e.g., early iron deficiency with concurrent B12 deficiency).
A patient with severe anaemia (Hb 6 g/dL) and MCV 85 fL is unstable — what immediate step? — Stabilise with blood transfusion while investigating cause.
Why might a recent blood transfusion mask the patient’s true MCV? — Donor red cells have normal size, diluting the patient’s abnormal indices.
What red‑cell index would you expect in sideroblastic anaemia and why? — Micro‑cytic with high RDW; defective haem synthesis leads to small, variable cells.
ai.title: Mean Cell Volume (MCV)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells and helps classify anaemia. It is calculated from a full blood count and guides further work‑up, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: MCV = (Hematocrit % × 10) ÷ RBC count (million/µL)
Normal range: 80–100 fL (may vary slightly by laboratory).
sections.p: Mean Cell Volume (MCV) is the arithmetic mean of the volume of individual erythrocytes, expressed in femtolitres (fL). It is derived from the haematocrit and red cell count on a complete blood count (CBC).

b: Micro‑cytic: <80 fL
Normo‑cytic: 80–100 fL
Macro‑cytic: >100 fL
sections.p: MCV itself is not staged, but it categorises anaemia into micro‑cytic, normo‑cytic, or macro‑cytic, directing the next diagnostic steps.

b: Micro‑cytic: iron deficiency (common in women, children, malaria‑related blood loss), chronic infection (TB, HIV), thalassaemia, sideroblastic anaemia.
Normo‑cytic: acute blood loss, haemolysis, early iron deficiency, chronic disease (TB, HIV, renal disease).
Macro‑cytic: folate deficiency (poor diet, malabsorption), vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, malabsorption), alcohol excess, drug‑induced (e.g., zidovudine), hypothyroidism.
sections.p: The underlying cause of an abnormal MCV depends on the size category and local disease prevalence.

b: Micro‑cytic: often chronic fatigue, spoon nails, pica.
Macro‑cytic: neurological signs (paresthesia) if B12 deficient, smooth tongue, easy bruising.
sections.p: Patients present with symptoms of anaemia—fatigue, dyspnoea, pallor—plus clues to the aetiology such as pica (iron deficiency), glossitis (B12/folate), or jaundice (haemolysis).
Beyond the CBC, targeted tests clarify the cause of an abnormal MCV.

t.b: Is iron stores depleted? Low ferritin confirms iron‑deficiency anaemia.
What does cell morphology show? Micro‑cytes, hypochromia, or macro‑ovalocytes guide diagnosis.
Is B12 deficient? Low level supports macro‑cytic anaemia due to B12.
Is folate deficient? Low level points to folate‑related macro‑cytosis.
Is the marrow responding? High count suggests haemolysis or blood loss; low suggests production problem.

t.a: Stool occult blood (if ferritin low and resources limited)
t.b: Is there gastrointestinal blood loss? Positive test supports iron loss.

b: MCV < 60 fL with Hb < 7 g/dL – risk of cardiac failure.
Macro‑cytosis with neurological signs – risk of irreversible neuropathy.
Persistent unexplained anaemia – consider malignancy or bone‑marrow failure.
sections.p: Severe anaemia or untreated deficiencies can be life‑threatening.

b: Avoid drugs that worsen macro‑cytosis (e.g., zidovudine) unless essential; switch if possible.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then correct the anaemia.

b: Iron therapy: repeat Hb and MCV; look for rise in Hb > 1 g/dL.
B12/folate: expect MCV to fall into normal range within 4–6 weeks.
Educate on diet rich in iron (meat, beans), folate (leafy greens), and B12 (animal products).
sections.p: Re‑check CBC after 2–4 weeks of therapy; monitor for response and side‑effects.

b: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH) – measures average haemoglobin per cell.
Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW) – measures variation in cell size.
sections.p: MCV is sometimes mixed up with other red‑cell indices.

b: Cold agglutinins – can falsely raise MCV.
Severe hyperlipidaemia – may cause spuriously low MCV on some analysers.
Recent transfusion – masks patient’s own MCV.
sections.p: Certain conditions alter MCV without true size change.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea, chest pain, or syncope with anaemia
Unexplained rapid fall in Hb despite treatment
